:::{#thm-normal-density-max}
#### The maximum of the normal density

If $X \sim \ndist{\mean, \ss}$ ([normal distribution](random-variables.qmd#def-normal)),
then its [density](random-variables.qmd#def-pdf) is largest at $x = \mean$,
where it equals:

$$\max_x \p(X=x) = \frac{1}{\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}}$$

:::

::: proof

For each $x \in \reals$, the quantity $u(x) \eqdef (x-\mean)^2 / (2\ss)$ is at least $0$,
and it equals $0$ only at $x = \mean$.
The factor $\ef{-u(x)}$ of the [density](random-variables.qmd#def-pdf) is at most $1$:

$$
\ba
-u(x)
&\le 0
&& \text{(a square is non-negative, and } 2\ss > 0 \text{)} \\
\ef{-u(x)}
&\le \ef{0}
&& \text{(} \text{e}^t \text{ is increasing in } t \text{)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(} \text{e}^0 = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

Multiplying both sides by $1 / (\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}) > 0$ keeps their order:

$$
\ba
\p(X=x)
&= \frac{1}{\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}} \ef{-u(x)}
&& \text{(normal density)} \\
&\le \frac{1}{\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}}
&& \text{(} \ef{-u(x)} \le 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

Equality holds at $x = \mean$, where $u(x) = 0$, so the density peaks there.

:::
